title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial (N=150 synthetic intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to measure whether constrained prompting plus deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback (generate→verify→repair; at most one repair) increases verifier-level semantic correctness for natural-language → low-level network-configuration translation. Model: gpt-5-mini; verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5; adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Results (confirmatory): baseline = 149/150 (99.333%); guarded = 150/150 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.0066667 (0.67 percentage points); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150); median revision iterations = 0 (IQR = 0). Interpretation: on this preregistered synthetic corpus the guarded workflow yielded a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement over an already near-ceiling baseline. We bound this empirical outcome to the synthetic corpus, single model, shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, and deterministic validator, and we draw a methodological recommendation: include a short pilot baseline-calibration step in preregistered NetOps trials to avoid ceiling effects that invalidate power assumptions.

sections.introduction:
Natural-language intent interfaces seek to reduce NetOps friction by translating operator intents into concrete, verifier-checkable low-level configuration sequences. Prior surveys and empirical work report that LLMs can produce useful configuration templates but often produce syntactic errors, omissions, or unsafe sequences requiring downstream correction [1], motivating generate→verify→repair defensive architectures that integrate deterministic verifiers with model outputs [2], [3]. Security analyses further motivate runtime gating because textual claims can map directly to tool calls in agentic LLM pipelines, producing claim-to-action vulnerabilities [4], [5].

Research question. Building on this literature, we preregistered and executed the confirmatory question: Does constrained prompting (structured templates + explicit semantic slots) combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase verifier-level semantic correctness of NL→configuration translation compared to an unconstrained baseline under a paired design? The experiment, analysis plan, and execution contract were frozen before observing outcomes (preregistration id: study_cand_2026_b2_v1; preregistration SHA-256 reported in the Disclosure Statement).

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial using a deterministic network validator as the primary oracle and a synthetic verifier-capable task bank; (2) an artifactized execution with complete accounting (planned paired episodes = 300; completed = 300; complete pairs = 150; model_calls_used = 151; repair invocations = 1) that implements shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) an artifact-grounded empirical result showing a negligible guarded-vs-baseline marginal benefit under the chosen semantics and model; (4) concrete methodological guidance (pilot baseline calibration, explicit generation semantics, and repair-budget sensitivity) for future preregistered NetOps trials.
sections.related_work:
We synthesize three adjacent strands relevant to verifier-guided NetOps workflows. First, intent-to-configuration research documents the difficulty of converting free-text operator intents into verifier-sound artifacts and reports modest semantic-correctness on public benchmarks; these studies motivate structured prompting and verifier-in-the-loop designs [1]. Second, generator-plus-verifier and iterative repair approaches in infrastructure-as-code and configuration repair (including verifier-guided training or policy-guided repair) report measurable correctness gains in curated settings [2], [6]. Third, security analyses of agentic LLM pipelines document claim-to-action and prompt-injection vulnerabilities that motivate auditable gating and deterministic checks before tool invocation [4], [5].

Positioning. Our trial operationalizes a narrowly specified guarded intervention (constrained prompt + at most one deterministic repair) and a paired design under shared_initial_candidate semantics so the numeric outcome measures the marginal benefit of a single repair applied to the identical initial sampled candidate. This differs from prior studies that (a) used independent per-condition sampling, (b) allowed multi-iteration repairs, (c) tested multiple models, or (d) evaluated different task difficulty distributions; such differences explain why prior reported gains can exceed ours despite consistent underlying motivation [2], [6].
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered as study_cand_2026_b2_v1 and frozen prior to observing any model outputs (preregistration SHA-256 = aea996afce45e3798345f6e32ae6c347456f103ecdb84fc36e27bb486a329399). The confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary hypothesis testing used an exact two-sided McNemar test; 95% bootstrap percentile confidence intervals were computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729).

Execution semantics and the shared_initial_candidate clarification. The adapter enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and that sampled candidate was used to evaluate both baseline and guarded conditions. The guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call only if the deterministic validator failed that initial candidate. Consequently, the observed baseline success rate measures the validity of a single initial sampled candidate; the guarded vs baseline contrast therefore isolates the marginal effect of at most one repair applied to the identical initial candidate.

Task bank, sampling, and inclusion rules. Confirmatory sample: N=150 distinct synthetic intents generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Tasks span four intent families (reachability/isolation, ACL-like changes, VLAN/MTU sequences, uplink switchover patterns) and are restricted to verifier-capable small topologies (4–32 nodes). A rule-based ambiguity detector and parser/verifier-coverage checks were applied deterministically prior to model calls. For this run no confirmatory exclusions occurred (exclusions = 0).

Model, validator, and runtime sampling semantics (reviewer clarification). Declared model = gpt-5-mini (provider record: openai_responses); deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0). The archived execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null (unset). Important literal clarification required by review: temperature = null was not interpreted as enforcing deterministic (temperature=0) sampling; no fixed sampling temperature or fixed random seed was enforced, and therefore model outputs may be nondeterministic across independent API sessions. All per-call runtime sampling metadata and provider-call logs are archived in the execution bundle.

Adapter, repair budget, and control constraints. Adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 enforced exactly one initial model call per intent and at most one repair call (planned episodes = 300; maximum_model_calls = 300). Each model call executed in an isolated API session; session isolation and per-call metadata were recorded and audited. The repair budget was therefore capped at a single repair invocation per intent, consistent with the preregistered generate→verify→repair protocol.

Scoring and analysis plan. The deterministic validator applied a full-intent-constraint validation rule returning a boolean pass/fail and a normalized configuration text. Primary analysis used an exact two-sided McNemar test on the paired contingency table with 10,000 bootstrap resamples (seed = 1729) to produce a 95% percentile CI. Handling of missingness followed the preregistered complete-pair strategy; no missing or unscorable pairs occurred. All analysis code and artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, analysis logs) are archived.

sections.discussion:
Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch. The preregistered power analysis targeted detecting an absolute improvement ≈15 percentage points with N=150 under an assumed lower baseline. Observed baseline initial-candidate success = 149/150 (≈99.33%), producing a ceiling effect that made the preregistered contrast uninformative for large effects. This outcome empirically illustrates that short pilot baseline calibration is necessary in preregistered NetOps trials to align task difficulty with model competence and preserve statistical power.

Interpretation under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because the same initial sampled candidate was shared across conditions, the guarded pipeline's only channel to change the paired outcome was the single allowed repair applied to that same sample. The measured paired difference is therefore a direct bound on the marginal benefit obtainable from at most one repair applied to an identical initial generation; larger observed differences in prior work are compatible when alternative semantics (independent per-condition sampling) or larger repair budgets are used.

Operational implications beyond binary pass/fail. Even when a guarded pipeline yields negligible incremental verifier pass rates on a synthetic corpus, deterministic verifier integration still provides operational value not captured by a single binary endpoint: standardized auditable verdicts, explicit repair prompts for operator dashboards, machine-checkable gating points for human approval, and durable artifacts for post-change forensics. These non-statistical benefits are important when considering design trade-offs between strict gating and automation throughput.

Relation to prior empirical work. Our artifact-grounded measurement does not contradict prior demonstrations of larger repair gains [2], [6]; those studies typically involved lower baseline competence, richer repair channels, multi-iteration feedback, or different sampling semantics. The current contribution is a narrowly bounded empirical measurement: a single-repair guarded pipeline under shared_initial_candidate semantics, gpt-5-mini, and a deterministic validator on a synthetic verifier-capable task bank.

Threats to validity and diagnostic artifacts. Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate semantics were chosen to isolate marginal repair effect but do not capture inter-condition sampling variance. Construct validity: verifier pass/fail is a machine-checkable proxy for semantic correctness and depends on mapping code and validator coverage; the execution bundle includes deterministic unit-tests for mapping code run pre-execution. External validity: single-model (gpt-5-mini), synthetic tasks, and small topologies (4–32 nodes) limit generalization to production WANs, heterogeneous vendor CLIs, or multi-model ensembles. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions were invalidated by the high baseline, producing an exact McNemar p = 1.0 and a tight bootstrap CI that reflects limited room for improvement under these conditions.

Practical recommendations. Based on the artifact-grounded outcome we recommend (1) a short pilot to estimate baseline initial-candidate correctness with the selected model/prompts before locking sample size; (2) explicit declaration of generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate vs independent sampling) aligned with the estimand of interest; (3) preregistered sensitivity analyses over repair budgets (one vs multiple repairs); and (4) pre-execution mapping unit-tests and verifier-coverage checks archived prior to model calls to prevent contamination by translator or verifier gaps.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial comparing free-text baseline prompting to constrained-template prompting plus one verifier-guided repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. On the archived synthetic corpus with gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator the guarded pipeline increased verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (0.67 pp), a numerically tiny and statistically non-significant difference (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The primary scientific lesson is methodological: preregistered LLM-for-NetOps trials should include pilot baseline calibration so task difficulty and sample size preserve inferential power. Technically, our artifacts bound the marginal benefit of a single-repair guarded pipeline under shared_initial_candidate semantics; evaluating independent-sampling semantics, larger repair budgets, model diversity, and production-scale topologies remains important future work.

limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to at most one guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than the pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned detectable effect = 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures deterministic validator pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
